title: Tâi-gí: The Language That Belonged at Home—and Deserved a Place Everywhere
deck: From decades of Mandarin-centered schooling and the marginalization of local languages to renewed recognition, education, and the effort to pass Taiwanese Taigi to another generation, this is a story about the cost of linguistic inequality—and the people working to change it.

sections.heading: When the Language of Home Was No Longer Welcome at School
sections.body:
Imagine a child growing up surrounded by a language.

It is heard in the kitchen, in conversations between neighbors, in the voices of grandparents, at markets, and during family gatherings. It carries familiar expressions, affection, humor, arguments, and the countless small exchanges that make a place feel like home.

Then the child enters school.

There, another language is given authority.

The language spoken at home may be discouraged, corrected, or treated as unsuitable for education. Speaking it can attract disapproval or disciplinary consequences. Learning, achievement, and opportunity increasingly become associated with the language favored by the state.

The child has not suddenly forgotten the language of home.

But the institutions shaping that child's future have begun teaching a different lesson about its value.

For generations of people in Taiwan, this tension formed part of the experience of living under Mandarin-centered language policies.

Taiwanese Taigi—commonly known as *Tâi-gí* and also called Taiwanese Hokkien or Taiwanese Southern Min—is a living language with deep roots in the everyday life and cultural history of Taiwan.

It has been used in family conversations, traditional performance, religious life, storytelling, music, and ordinary communication across generations.

Yet after 1945, and particularly during the decades of authoritarian Nationalist rule, government policy gave Mandarin a privileged position in education and public institutions.

Other languages spoken in Taiwan, including Taigi, Hakka varieties, and Indigenous languages, faced marginalization through a system that promoted Mandarin as the shared national language.

The consequences reached beyond schools.

They affected which languages children felt comfortable speaking, which languages parents believed would help their families advance, and which forms of cultural expression received institutional support.

But Taigi did not disappear.

It continued through the people who spoke it, the communities that sustained its cultural life, and later generations who challenged the unequal position of Taiwan's languages.

Today, Taigi is receiving renewed attention through education, language policy, dictionaries, media, digital tools, and community-led efforts to strengthen its use.

The work is far from finished.

But its purpose reaches beyond preserving a record of the past.

**It is about ensuring that the language people inherited can also become a language they confidently pass on.**

---

sections.heading: 01 — When a Familiar Language Lost Its Place in Public Life
sections.body:
### The pressure on Taigi was not simply a matter of changing vocabulary. It reflected changing political power.

To understand the modern history of Taiwanese Taigi, it is necessary to understand the political transformation Taiwan experienced during the twentieth century.

Taiwan had been under Japanese colonial rule from 1895 until 1945. During that period, Japanese-language education and assimilation policies had already shaped the island's linguistic environment.

After Japan's surrender in 1945, Taiwan came under the administration of the Republic of China, governed by the Chinese Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang.

The new authorities promoted Mandarin as the national language.

This was not merely an educational decision about which language children should study.

Mandarin became closely associated with state authority, public administration, official communication, and advancement within the institutions controlled by the government.

Taiwan, however, was not a monolingual society.

Its population included speakers of Taigi, Hakka varieties, numerous Indigenous languages, and other languages shaped by the island's complex history.

The government's Mandarin-centered approach did not give those languages an equivalent place in public life.

### A National Language Policy With Unequal Consequences

Mandarin promotion became particularly consequential within Taiwan's authoritarian political system.

Martial law was imposed in 1949 and remained in effect until 1987. During this period, the state exercised extensive control over political activity, education, and public expression.

Language policy formed part of that wider institutional environment.

Schools became important instruments for promoting Mandarin, while opportunities to use local languages in formal education were restricted.

Taigi-speaking children could arrive at school fluent in a language that had shaped their earliest understanding of the world, only to encounter an educational system organized around another.

Accounts of Taiwan's Mandarin-only schooling era describe disciplinary practices used to discourage students from speaking local languages. Experiences varied between schools and generations, and specific punishments should be supported by documented testimony rather than assumed to have occurred everywhere.

But the broader educational hierarchy is clear.

Mandarin carried official authority.

Taigi and other local languages were marginalized in institutional settings.

That distinction could affect a child's understanding of language, knowledge, and belonging.

**A language did not have to be formally forbidden in every private conversation for its speakers to receive the message that it belonged outside the places where their futures were being decided.**

### The Human Cost of Linguistic Stigma

A child learning through an unfamiliar or less familiar language faces more than a question of vocabulary.

They must navigate expectations about which language is appropriate, which forms of speech are respected, and how they should communicate with teachers and authorities.

For children who spoke Taigi naturally at home, school could reinforce the idea that Mandarin was the language of education and success, while Taigi occupied a lower social position.

That hierarchy could follow children beyond their school years.

As they entered employment, formed relationships, and raised families, the institutional advantages of Mandarin could influence their decisions about which language to use.

Parents naturally wanted their children to succeed.

Some increasingly emphasized Mandarin at home because it was the language of schooling and professional opportunity.

Others continued using Taigi while ensuring their children acquired Mandarin.

These decisions were made under changing political, social, and economic conditions.

They should not be interpreted as proof that families no longer cared about their ancestral or community languages.

A parent may love the language inherited from previous generations while believing that another language offers a child greater protection or opportunity.

That is one of the most difficult consequences of linguistic inequality.

**The pressure placed upon a language in public institutions can eventually change the language spoken between parents and children.**

And once that pattern changes across generations, restoring everyday transmission becomes far more difficult than changing a law.

---

sections.heading: 02 — A Language That Continued Outside the Institutions of Power
sections.body:
### Taigi remained alive because people continued to speak, perform, create, and maintain relationships through it.

It would be misleading to suggest that Taiwanese Taigi simply disappeared during the decades of Mandarin-centered education.

It did not.

Taigi remained part of family and community life. It continued to be heard in markets, neighborhoods, religious settings, traditional performing arts, and many forms of informal communication.

The language also retained a connection to artistic and cultural traditions, including Taiwanese opera, commonly known as *koa-á-hì*, and other forms of performance and storytelling.

These traditions were not merely historical decorations.

They provided settings in which the language could continue carrying emotion, humor, narrative, and cultural expression.

But survival within families and cultural settings did not mean that restrictions on education, broadcasting, and public institutions were harmless.

A language can remain widely understood while becoming less common among younger speakers.

It can remain familiar in music and performance while fewer children use it naturally with their friends.

And it can retain enormous cultural importance while becoming increasingly difficult to pass from one generation to the next.

### The Difference Between Understanding and Speaking

One of the most important challenges in language transmission is the distinction between understanding a language and being able to use it confidently.

A child may grow up hearing grandparents speak Taigi.

They may recognize familiar expressions, understand routine conversations, or associate the language with particular family members.

But if the child is expected to answer primarily in Mandarin, opportunities to develop active speaking ability may be limited.

Over time, an asymmetry can emerge.

An older generation speaks Taigi fluently.

A younger generation understands more than it speaks.

The next generation may grow up with even less regular exposure.

This pattern does not describe every Taiwanese family, and it should not be treated as inevitable.

But it illustrates how a language can lose strength in everyday transmission while remaining familiar and emotionally important.

A language's vitality depends on more than whether people recognize it.

It depends on whether people can use it to express themselves, form relationships, and participate in daily life.

### Cultural Survival Was Not Institutional Equality

For Taigi-speaking communities, maintaining the language through periods of official marginalization represented continuity and resilience.

But that continuity should not be romanticized.

Families and cultural practitioners should not have had to compensate for the unequal treatment of their language in education and public institutions.

Nor should their persistence be used to imply that state policies caused little damage.

The issue was not simply whether Taigi could still be heard somewhere.

It was whether its speakers had meaningful opportunities to use it across the full range of social life.

A language of home deserves more than permission to remain at home.

It deserves the opportunity to function in education, public communication, creative expression, and the institutions that shape contemporary society.

---

sections.heading: 03 — From Mandarin Dominance Toward Linguistic Recognition
sections.body:
### Changing the legal position of a language is an important step. Changing its everyday reality takes longer.

Taiwan's transition toward democratization created new opportunities to challenge longstanding language hierarchies.

The lifting of martial law in 1987 was a major political milestone, although the broader transition and expansion of civic freedoms continued over subsequent years.

Language rights and cultural recognition became increasingly important subjects of public discussion.

Communities, educators, researchers, writers, and advocates pressed for greater support for languages that had been marginalized under Mandarin-centered policies.

These efforts formed part of a wider recognition that Taiwan's linguistic diversity was not an obstacle to national life.

It was part of the society's history and present.

### Bringing Local Languages Back Into Education

An important change came in 2001, when local-language learning entered Taiwan's reformed school curriculum.

This created formal opportunities for students to study languages that earlier educational policies had marginalized.

For Taigi, the significance was substantial.

A language once discouraged or excluded in many classrooms could now be approached as a legitimate subject of education.

But the difference between teaching a language and sustaining a community that uses it remained.

A weekly lesson may introduce vocabulary, pronunciation, and cultural material.

Developing confident speakers requires repeated opportunities to listen, converse, read, and use the language across meaningful situations.

Teachers need preparation.

Schools need suitable resources.

Students need reasons to continue using the language beyond formal instruction.

And families need support if they wish to transmit it at home.

Educational recognition creates possibilities.

Making those possibilities effective requires sustained commitment.

### 2019 — Recognition of Taiwan's National Languages

In January 2019, Taiwan promulgated the **Development of National Languages Act**.

The law established a broader framework recognizing Taiwan's natural languages and Taiwan Sign Language as national languages, with provisions intended to support preservation, development, education, and transmission.

The significance of this change should not be understated.

It marked a departure from the earlier institutional hierarchy that privileged Mandarin while giving limited public recognition to other languages.

The law acknowledged the importance of protecting linguistic diversity and creating responsibilities for support.

But legal recognition is not the same as evidence that intergenerational transmission has recovered.

It does not automatically produce enough teachers, restore every family language pattern, or ensure that young people will choose to speak Taigi in everyday life.

A language may gain greater recognition while continuing to face social pressures.

**Changing a language's legal status can open a door. Keeping that door open requires people, resources, and opportunities for meaningful use.**

---

sections.heading: 04 — Rebuilding the Conditions for a Language to Thrive
sections.body:
### Revitalization does not mean returning to a frozen version of the past.

Taiwanese Taigi is not important only because it preserves older cultural traditions.

It is a language that can be used to discuss contemporary life, create new literature, communicate digitally, and express experiences that previous generations could not have anticipated.

Supporting its future therefore requires more than documenting historical vocabulary.

It requires materials and institutions that make the language practical for modern speakers.

### Teachers, Dictionaries, and Language Resources

Taiwan's national languages development planning for 2022–2026 identified priorities including teacher preparation, educational resources, language documentation, media, and digital tools.

The Ministry of Education also provides language-reference materials, including a dictionary of frequently used Taiwanese Taigi.

Such resources have practical importance.

They help learners check vocabulary and written forms rather than relying on approximation or substituting Mandarin expressions.

They can assist teachers developing educational materials and support efforts to make language learning more accessible.

But resources alone cannot create a living language community.

A dictionary can explain a word.

It cannot replace the conversations through which people learn when, why, and how to use it.

Language learning is most meaningful when written materials are connected to authentic speech, cultural context, and opportunities for interaction.

### The Role of Media and Creative Life

Modern media also offers possibilities for strengthening Taigi's visibility and use.

Broadcasting, music, film, literature, podcasts, and online communication can help younger generations encounter the language outside formal lessons.

Creative work is especially important because it allows speakers to express contemporary experiences.

A language should not be confined to old songs or traditional ceremonies.

It should also be available for discussing everyday frustrations, relationships, humor, technology, politics, and the future.

That does not diminish its cultural heritage.

It demonstrates its continued relevance.

When younger speakers hear a language used naturally in contemporary settings, they encounter more than a symbol of the past.

They encounter a means of expression that can belong to their own lives.

### The Importance of Family Transmission

Institutional support can help create opportunities, but the transmission of a language often depends on relationships between people.

Children need to hear language being used.

They need opportunities to respond, ask questions, and develop confidence.

Grandparents, parents, caregivers, teachers, and other speakers all have roles in creating those opportunities.

This is particularly important where earlier generations experienced pressure to prioritize Mandarin.

The goal should not be to blame families for decisions made under unequal circumstances.

It should be to make different decisions possible for those who wish to pass Taigi to their children today.

That may involve language classes, accessible learning materials, community gatherings, media, family activities, or opportunities for children and adults to use Taigi together.

There is no single path for every household.

But the principle is consistent.

**A language grows stronger when people are given the opportunity to use it with those who matter to them.**

---

sections.heading: 05 — Writing Taigi: More Than One Way to Put a Living Language on the Page
sections.body:
### A language cannot be fully supported in digital life if people cannot write it accurately.

Taiwanese Taigi presents important questions for digital writing because it is represented through more than one writing convention.

Materials may use Chinese characters, romanization, or a combination of both.

Among the romanization systems used for Taigi are **Pe̍h-ōe-jī (POJ)** and **Tâi-uân Lô-má-jī Phing-im Hong-àn (Tâi-lô)**.

These systems have their own conventions.

Their distinctions should not be ignored or casually combined.

A written passage should identify which convention it follows, especially when presented as educational material.

### Why Tone Marks Matter

Taigi is a tonal language.

Tone is an essential part of its spoken linguistic system, and romanized writing conventions use particular marks or notation to represent tonal distinctions.

For learners encountering written Taigi, unfamiliar diacritics may require a different keyboard layout, input method, or additional technical preparation.

That difficulty should not be solved by simply removing the marks from words that require them.

The marks contribute to the accuracy of the written form.

Similarly, when practising Chinese-character Taigi, a Mandarin sentence should not be substituted merely because both languages can be written using Chinese characters.

Sharing parts of a writing system does not make two languages interchangeable.

A learner can become highly literate in written Mandarin without necessarily learning to speak, read, or write Taigi.

That distinction is one of the reasons accurate language labeling matters.

### Why Digital Tools Are Part of the Wider Picture

Keyboards, dictionaries, input methods, digital corpora, and educational software may appear less emotionally significant than the histories of schools and language policies.

But they help determine how easily people can use a language in contemporary life.

If accurate spelling is difficult to enter, learners may struggle with written practice.

If digital resources are limited, teachers may have fewer materials available.

If software assumes that every Chinese-character passage is Mandarin, the distinct linguistic identity of Taigi can be obscured.

Better digital support cannot replace fluent speakers or everyday conversation.

But it can remove practical barriers.

A language's place in the digital world matters because digital communication is increasingly part of how people maintain relationships, learn, and share knowledge.

Taigi belongs in those spaces on its own terms.

---

sections.heading: 06 — Why WPMTest Includes Taiwanese Taigi
sections.body:
### A typing exercise cannot repair language suppression. It can encourage a more careful first encounter.

WPMTest's Living Languages Series explores the histories of languages affected by unequal institutions, social pressure, and changing patterns of transmission.

Taiwanese Taigi belongs in this collection because its history demonstrates how government language policy can shape what children learn, which languages receive institutional authority, and how families make decisions about the next generation.

Its contemporary revitalization efforts also show why legal recognition must be accompanied by education, linguistic resources, and opportunities for everyday use.

Our contribution is modest.

A typing website cannot undo the experiences of children who were discouraged from speaking their home languages.

It cannot replace the work of teachers, community advocates, language researchers, or families sustaining Taigi.

And it cannot measure whether someone has developed the ability to speak or understand the language.

What it can do is provide carefully sourced historical context, encourage accurate written practice, and direct readers toward appropriate language-learning resources.

For Taigi, the introductory pathway begins with language-name and character-copying activities, alongside the option to use independently verified text.

It does not yet claim to offer a speaker-reviewed collection of complete Taigi sentences.

Anyone preparing their own passages should identify the writing system, preserve the original spelling and tone marks, verify the language rather than assuming a Mandarin passage is equivalent, and ensure they have appropriate rights to use the material.

Where possible, written study should be paired with authentic audio, language instruction, and opportunities for conversation.

**The purpose is not to type Taigi faster. It is to recognize that a language once marginalized by institutions deserves accuracy, respect, and a meaningful place in modern life.**

---

sections.heading: Turning Points in Taiwanese Taigi's Story
sections.body:
**1895–1945 — Japanese Colonial Rule**

Taiwan is governed by Japan. Japanese-language education and assimilation policies influence the island's linguistic environment, including the public position of local languages.

**1945 — A New Political and Linguistic Order**

Following the end of Japanese rule, Taiwan comes under the administration of the Republic of China. The Nationalist government promotes Mandarin as the national language.

**1949–1987 — Martial Law and Mandarin-Centered Institutions**

During decades of authoritarian rule, Mandarin receives privileged institutional status while Taigi and other local languages face marginalization in education and public communication.

**1987 — Martial Law Is Lifted**

The lifting of martial law marks an important stage in Taiwan's political liberalization, creating conditions for broader public debate about language and cultural rights.

**2001 — Local Languages Enter the School Curriculum**

Educational reforms introduce local-language learning, opening new opportunities for students to study languages previously marginalized in formal education.

**2019 — Development of National Languages Act**

Taiwan promulgates legislation establishing a framework for the recognition, preservation, development, and support of its national languages.

**2022–2026 — National Languages Development Plan**

Government planning identifies priorities for education, language resources, media, teacher preparation, documentation, and digital support.

*These milestones are selected points in a longer history. The experiences of Taigi, Hakka, Indigenous-language, and other communities differ and should not be treated as identical. Policy milestones also do not, by themselves, establish whether language use has increased.*

---

sections.heading: Make Room for Taigi on Your Keyboard
sections.body:
Taiwanese Taigi deserves to be written accurately.

Materials may use Chinese characters, romanization, or mixed forms. Before beginning, identify the writing convention used by your source.

**Tâi-gí · Pe̍h-ōe-jī**

Preserve the tone marks, diacritics, and spelling required by the selected system.

For romanized passages, Tâi-lô and Pe̍h-ōe-jī should be clearly identified rather than silently combined. Keyboard tools should also preserve the intended Unicode characters and combining marks.

The WPMTest introductory pathway provides language-name and character-copying activities, alongside the option to practise with independently verified material.

**[Explore Taiwanese Taigi Character Practice →](https://wpmtest.app/language-revival/taiwanese-taigi/typing-test/)**

*Words per minute measures keyboard performance. It does not measure Taigi fluency, cultural knowledge, or community belonging.*

---

sections.heading: The Voice That Deserves to Be Heard in Every Generation
sections.body:
There is a profound difference between a language being familiar and a language being free to flourish.

For generations, Taigi remained present in Taiwanese homes, neighborhoods, cultural traditions, and everyday conversations.

But the institutions that shaped education and public life increasingly privileged Mandarin.

Children grew up navigating the distance between the language of home and the language associated with authority.

Families made difficult decisions within unequal circumstances.

Some patterns of intergenerational transmission weakened.

Those consequences cannot be dismissed as the ordinary passage of time.

They were shaped, in part, by political decisions about which languages deserved institutional support.

But Taigi's history does not end with exclusion.

People continued speaking it.

Cultural practitioners continued creating through it.

Families maintained relationships across generations through familiar words and expressions.

And later generations worked to challenge the unequal position of Taiwan's languages.

Today, Taigi has greater legal recognition, educational resources, dictionaries, media, and opportunities for learning than those earlier institutional arrangements allowed.

These achievements matter.

Yet they are not the same as a secure future.

A language cannot be sustained by recognition alone.

It needs children who can learn it, adults who can use it, teachers who can teach it, and communities where speaking it feels natural.

It needs opportunities to be heard not only in historical recordings or cultural performances, but in ordinary life.

The hope in Taigi's story is not that every problem has been solved.

It is that people are working to make possible what earlier generations were often discouraged from doing.

A grandparent can share a familiar expression.

A parent can choose to learn or strengthen the language.

A child can encounter Taigi in education and carry it into new conversations.

A writer, musician, or filmmaker can create something that belongs unmistakably to the present.

**The language once treated as out of place in classrooms now has people working to ensure it belongs in schools, homes, public life, and the future.**

That work is not complete.

But Taigi is not simply a voice from Taiwan's past.

**It is a familiar voice that deserves to be heard—and answered—by generations still to come.**

---

sections.heading: Sources, Photography, and Editorial Care
sections.body:
This article draws on the following government, educational, and language-resource materials:

1. [Taiwan Ministry of Education — Educational Reform and Authoritarian Education](https://english.moe.gov.tw/cp-117-21022-B8B67-1.html) — Historical context concerning Taiwanese education and authoritarian-era policies.

2. [Taiwan Executive Yuan — National Language and Hakka Legal Frameworks](https://www.ey.gov.tw/Goals/917B6A92037AFF1B) — Government information concerning language-recognition and development frameworks.

3. [Taiwan Executive Yuan — National Languages Development Plan](https://english.ey.gov.tw/News3/9E5540D592A5FECD/0ce73bb5-0330-4491-9fdb-9eb06f7114d3) — Policy priorities relating to language transmission, education, media, and digital resources.

4. [Taiwan Ministry of Education — Language Dictionaries and Resources](https://english.moe.gov.tw/np-33-1.html) — Official language-learning and reference resources.

5. [Taiwan Ministry of Education — Localized Education and Mother-Tongue Curriculum](https://english.moe.gov.tw/public/Attachment/012131727571.pdf) — Educational context concerning local-language learning.

**Recommended additional sources before publication:** Primary and scholarly documentation concerning Mandarin-only disciplinary practices in Taiwanese schools, Japanese colonial language education, the history of Taigi-language broadcasting, and intergenerational Taigi speaking trends.

### Photography

Shennong Street, Tainan, Taiwan.

Photograph: [Tze Chiang Hao](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%E7%A5%9E%E8%BE%B2%E8%A1%97_Shennong_Street_Tainan_City02.jpg) · [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0).

The photograph introduces a place associated with Taiwan's cultural life. It does not establish the language spoken by any individual shown or represent the experiences of all Taiwanese communities.

### Our Editorial Approach

This article distinguishes the institutional promotion of Mandarin from claims that every private use of Taigi was prohibited.

It recognizes that school practices, family experiences, and patterns of language transmission differed across places and generations.

Taiwanese Taigi, Mandarin, Hakka varieties, Indigenous languages, and Taiwan Sign Language are not interchangeable. Their histories, linguistic characteristics, and community priorities should be represented separately.

The article also distinguishes legal recognition and announced policy objectives from demonstrated improvements in everyday language use.

This is a source-based editorial history, not a claim of fluent-speaker or specialist endorsement. New Taigi sentence passages should receive appropriate review by people familiar with the relevant spoken variety and written convention.
